attendance at the Summer Concert Series ,National Night Out event, Door of Hope’s
Annual Community and Volunteer event, a Norwalk/Santa Fe Springs Soroptimist
Meeting, and the Southeast Water Coalition Meeting where they unanimously agreed to
support Norwalk’s work on the water wells. Mayor Perez reported on her attendance at
the State of the Nation, the League of California Cities Annual Installation, and the
Summer Concert Series and National Night Out event where she thanked staff, the Public
Safety Department, the Los Angeles County Sherriff’s, Los Angeles County Firefighters,
and the Santa Fe Springs Police for making the night a success.

United States of America National Junior Olympic Championships, National Night Out
2026, Summer Concerts 2026, and the “Bi-Weekly Review”. He also shared resources

Background:

The Political Reform Act requires that every local government agency conduct a biennial review
of its conflict of interest code to determine if it is accurate or whether the code should be
amended. The Fair Political Practices Commission (FPPC) is charged with enforcing the
provisions of the Political Reform Act and has adopted a Model Conflict of Interest Code which
is incorporated by reference in the City’s Conflict of Interest Code. The Model Code will be
amended by the FPPC from time to time to conform with any amendments to the Political Reform
Act.

The City Clerk, City Attorney, and department directors have reviewed the City’s current Conflict
of Interest Code to determine if any changes were necessary. Appendix A, of the attached
resolution includes changes that have occurred since the last amendment and are consistent
with the Fiscal Year 2026/27 Budget. The highlighted changes are those that have been made
through the budget process since the last Conflict of Interest Code was adopted in 2024.

Background:

On September 16, 2025, City Council approved a one-year agreement with The Merino Group
for crisis communications services following a competitive RFP process. The City received three
qualified proposals and interviewed all three firms. The Merino Group received the highest
average evaluation score, 97 points compared with 93 points for Communications LAB and SAE
Communications, and was selected as the preferred firm.

The original agreement authorized a $3,000 monthly retainer and maximum annual
compensation of $100,000, inclusive of separately billable crisis communications services, and
included an option to extend the agreement for one additional year. Under the proposed
amendment, as adopted by the Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget, the City would exercise that option
through September 4, 2027, eliminating the $3,000 monthly retainer and reduce the maximum
annual compensation from $100,000 to $50,000. Services would be billed only at the hourly
rates established in the original agreement.

The scope of work will supplement the City’s internal communications capacity during high-
impact, sensitive or fast-moving issues. The City’s Communications Department continues to
lead day-to-day messaging, public information, media coordination and community engagement.
The Merino Group provides specialized support through public sentiment monitoring, media
monitoring, issue analysis, strategic messaging recommendations and crisis communications
support when additional expertise or surge capacity is needed.

During the current term, The Merino Group provided work in several key areas consistent with
the approved scope of services.

Parks, development and community project monitoring. The Merino Group evaluated public
sentiment related to Hermosillo Park, Holifield Park, Norwalk Park, The Walk and other visible
community projects. Reports identified resident concerns involving transparency, public input,
project timing, traffic impacts, loss of familiar community space and access to park amenities.
Recommendations included citywide parks progress communications, project life cycle updates,
and inclusion of cost and funding details.

Media and regional issue monitoring. The Merino Group monitored traditional media
coverage and regional issues that could affect Norwalk residents or be associated with City
operations. Topics included regional transportation projects, public safety alerts, education and
labor issues, public health alerts, state laws, immigration enforcement posts and regional fiscal
pressures. These reports provided staff with analysis regarding City responsibilities and those
of county, state, school district, utility and law enforcement agencies.

Staff anticipate the need for specialized, surge-capacity support. The Communications
Department will continue to manage routine City communications, while outside support will be
requested when additional monitoring, analysis or specialized communications assistance is
warranted.

performed and billed only when requested by the City, and actual monthly expenditures will vary

Background:

Norwalk Municipal Code Chapter 10.10 establishes procedures for Norwalk residents to
apply for the installation of a blue curbed parking space, for exclusive use of a disabled
person, in front of or adjacent to their residence. The Department of Public Safety
received an application from Ms. Shamil Shammeem for the installation of an on-street
disabled parking space (blue curb) on the side of her residence, located at 14617
Dartmoor Avenue. The property is located mid-block on the east side of the 14600 block
of Dartmoor Avenue, between Barnwall Street and Graystone Avenue.

Ms. Shamil Shameem lives on the property with her mother and brother. There is one
vehicle registered on the property. The property has no available on-site parking due to
the addition of an ADU. The main residence has only a one-car garage and driveway,
which are reserved for and accessible only to the occupants of the front house. As a
result, the occupants of the ADU do not have access to any on-site parking and must
rely on street parking.

Mr. Shamil Shameem, resident of 14617 Dartmoor Avenue., is requesting the
installation of a blue curb adjacent to the residence to improve accessibility and safety.
The applicant does not drive; the applicant's mother is the primary caregiver and driver.
Currently, the applicant's mother parks on the street, which is often some distance from
the residence due to limited parking availability.

The applicant has autism, which affects the ability to recognize traffic hazards. When
walking between the parked vehicle and the residence, the applicant may attempt to run
toward the roadway without understanding the danger posed by oncoming traffic. A blue
curb adjacent to the residence would provide a closer, more accessible parking space,
helping to improve the applicant's safety and facilitate transportation to and from home.

SUBJECT: UPDATED URBAN FOREST MANAGEMENT PLAN AND RESOLUTION NO.
  26-52, AMENDING THE FISCAL YEAR 2026/27 BUDGET TO APPROPRIATE
  FUNDS FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF THE TREE PLANTING INITIATIVES
  IDENTIFIED IN THE UPDATED URBAN FOREST MANAGEMENT PLAN

Background:

The City's urban forest is a vital component of Norwalk's public infrastructure, providing
significant environmental, economic, and social benefits. Public trees improve air quality, reduce
urban heat, capture stormwater, enhance neighborhood aesthetics, support wildlife habitat, and
contribute to the overall quality of life for residents, businesses, and visitors.

In November 2014, City Council adopted the City’s first Urban Forest Management Plan (Plan),
establishing a long-term framework for the management, preservation, and enhancement of the
City's publicly maintained trees. Since its adoption, the City has implemented many of the Plan’s
recommendations through proactive tree maintenance, annual tree planting programs, Arbor
Day celebrations, and ongoing public education and outreach efforts. The 2014 Plan was
developed with a 20-year planning horizon while recognizing that periodic updates would be
necessary to address changes in the City's urban forest, evolving community priorities, and
advancements in industry best management practices.

Over the past decade, City’s urban forest has continued to mature, while advancements in urban
forestry practices, technology, environmental conditions, and climate resilience have
underscored the need to update the existing Plan. Consequently, the 2014 Plan no longer
accurately reflects the City's current tree inventory, industry standards, or long-term urban
forestry priorities.
 City Council  September 1, 2026
Urban Forest Management Plan Update  Page No. 2

To address these changes, the City retained West Coast Arborists, Inc. to prepare an updated
Plan. The updated Plan provides comprehensive framework for managing, preserving, and
expanding Norwalk's publicly maintained urban forest while incorporating current industry
standards, updated inventory data, canopy assessments, and implementation strategies. The
Plan is intended to serve as a living document that will guide future tree planting, maintenance,
preservation, and management practices while remaining adaptable to changing environmental
conditions, community needs, and evolving best management practices.

The updated inventory identified approximately 16,164 publicly maintained trees representing
252 species, 148 genera, and 51 plant families. Approximately 82% of the City's trees are in
good condition, reflecting decades of proactive maintenance and stewardship. The inventory
also identified more than 10,000 vacant planting sites, presenting significant opportunities to
expand the City's urban tree canopy.

The Plan recommends increasing the City's tree canopy by an average of 3% every 10 years
through strategic tree planting, preservation of mature trees, and continued investment in
proactive maintenance. It also establishes implementation priorities, planting strategies,
maintenance standards, public education initiatives, and long-term goals that will guide the City's
urban forestry program for years to come.

In addition to establishing technical standards and implementation strategies, the Plan
emphasizes the importance of continued public education and community participation. The City
currently conducts annual outreach initiatives, including Arbor Day events, volunteer tree
planting opportunities, and other community programs that promote the value of Norwalk's urban
forest. The updated Plan builds upon these successful efforts by encouraging continued public
awareness, stewardship, and community involvement in maintaining a healthy and resilient, and
sustainable urban forest.

Benefits of the Updated Plan:
  • Establishes a long-term vision for the City's urban forest.
  • Improves consistency in tree planting and maintenance.
  • Expands tree canopy and climate resilience.
  • Improves species diversity.
  • Supports future grant opportunities.
  • Provides a framework for long-term budgeting and planning.

Discussion:

During the July 21, 2026, Study Session, City Council expressed general support for the Plan
and directed staff to incorporate additional implementation strategies prior to adoption.
Specifically, City Council emphasized expanding youth engagement by identifying meanable
opportunities to partner with local schools and involve students in tree planting activities and

SUBJECT: ACCEPTANCE OF THE 2025 SEWER MASTER PLAN

Background:

The City’s sewer system serves the area consisting of all lands within its corporate boundaries
(9.35 square miles) and provides sewer collection service to a population of approximately
98,100. The existing sewer collection system is comprised of approximately 163 miles (860,640
linear feet) of mostly gravity sewers of varying diameter; 2,480 sewer manholes; 26 sewer
siphons; and three sewage lift stations.

The previous 2014 Sanitary Sewer Master Plan (SMP) was completed and accepted by City
Council in 2015. SMP’s are intended to be used to provide guidance and recommendations for
improvements to system operations and maintenance; timely system improvements to ensure
uninterrupted and compliant services; identify and recommend future system capital
improvements; and account for future private development and associated system demands.

Due to the length of time since the 2014 SMP was completed, and the condition of the existing
data, staff determined it was best to prepare a new 2025 SMP instead of performing an update.
Public Services Utilities staff sought qualified and experienced engineering consulting firms to
prepare the 2025 SMP.

In April 2024, the City awarded a professional services agreement to Psomas to prepare the
2025 SMP. The scope of work included but was not limited to:

  Task 1 - Project Management and Meetings
  Task 2 - Review Existing Plans, Policies and Procedures

  Task 3 - GAP Analysis, Plan and Standards and Procedures Update or Development
  Task 4 - Flow Monitoring/Develop and Calibrate Sewer System Hydraulic Model
  Task 5 - Review Overflow Emergency Response Plan
  Task 6 - Draft and Final Updated SMP

These SMP tasks were to achieve the following goals:

  •  Collect and review of all data significant to and thorough completion of the SMP and sewer
  hydraulic model. Coordination with relevant agencies such as Los Angeles County
  Department of Public Works and Los Angeles County Sanitation District to acquire all
  data

  •  Submit a Technical Memorandum to identify and provide rationale for flow monitoring
  locations throughout the City

  •  Develop key system data to be used in the development of Sewer Impact Fees

  •  Provide a preliminary and final 2025 SMP that identifies deficiencies in the system and
  includes a prioritized 10-year plan (2025 – 2030/35) of all recommended alternatives for
  improvement of sewer facilities, cost estimates, and estimated project durations

  •  Develop a new sewer hydraulic model to identify peak flow factors and flow patterns,
  assess capacity constraints, and potential limitations for future development

  •  Conduct site investigations, as needed, to confirm information from existing reports and
  records

Once completed, staff reviewed and determined that the Plan provides a comprehensive
evaluation of the City’s sewer collection system, identifies capital improvements necessary to
maintain reliable service and mitigate or prevent sewer system overflows, and establishes a
framework for future planning.

Additionally, the system mapping data generated by this Plan will be uploaded and utilized for
the citywide Geographic Information System (GIS) system, allowing for timely and accurate
access to information which will facilitate and coordinate both future capital improvement projects
as well as private developments.
